profiles.meeting_scenario: At LedgerLoop, a SaaS company that sells workflow automation tools to enterprise customers, a staff platform architect and a senior product manager meet to brainstorm ideas for a CTO-offsite proposal: adding a serverless execution option so customers can run small event-driven functions inside workflows instead of provisioning always-on workers. The context is a two-week window to shape a prototype concept and a narrative that connects current serverless industry trends to a plausible internal product direction. The agenda is to generate and narrow candidate prototype approaches, decide what the first demo should implicitly prove, and identify which prior internal experiments can be reused. The expected outcome is a short list of prototype ingredients and a shared-sounding plan for what the 'MVP' should demonstrate to leadership and a potential design partner.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: Cloud runtime design, multi-tenant isolation, distributed systems, platform reliability
members.background: Priya has spent six years building LedgerLoop's internal execution infrastructure and recently led a Firecracker-based proof of concept for running untrusted customer code with strong isolation.
members.private_state: Priya wants any brainstormed direction to stay close to infrastructure the platform team can defend in a later security review, and she is trying to avoid a flashy demo that creates commitments around operational guarantees the current platform cannot actually meet.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'cold start,' they usually mean the runtime/container initialization cost after the request has already reached the execution layer, not upstream gateway or secret-fetch overhead.
An MVP for customer code execution is not credible unless the first end-to-end path already includes baseline platform concerns like secret injection, logging, and rollback hooks.

A convincing 'pay-as-you-go' story is mainly about eliminating pre-provisioned compute and showing better marginal cost on bursty workloads, even if some shared control-plane services still have steady cost.
The 'spring sandbox' everyone references is the March Firecracker executor prototype built by platform infrastructure.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: Developer-platform product strategy, enterprise workflow tooling, pilot programs with design partners
members.background: Alex came from an API-platform startup and now owns the roadmap for how external developers extend LedgerLoop workflows; he recently gathered customer feedback on demand for lighter-weight compute options inside integrations.
members.private_state: Alex wants a clean customer-facing story for the CTO offsite and hopes to secure a design partner quickly, so he is quietly steering toward the smallest demoable slice that makes serverless sound simple, modern, and economically intuitive.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'cold start,' they usually mean the full user-visible delay from event arrival to the first successful response, including auth, secret lookup, and network attachment.
An MVP should be the narrowest possible upload-trigger-run demo, while existing account auth, monitoring, and other platform services can remain implicit and out of scope.
A real 'pay-as-you-go' promise means customers should see essentially zero idle cost in the pilot story, with no always-on components that need explaining in pricing conversations.
The 'spring sandbox' being reused is the April Knative-based demo environment assembled by solutions engineering for the partner summit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the prototype needs an acceptable 'cold-start' story, ideally under a few hundred milliseconds.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means execution-layer startup time: sandbox boot, runtime init, and handler readiness once the invocation has already been routed to the worker environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means end-to-end first-invocation delay experienced by a customer flow, including API gateway handling, auth, secret retrieval, network setup, and runtime startup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Cold start is a standard industry term that both use fluently, and each assumes the other's frame is the obvious one for their shared serverless discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to focus on one 'MVP' or 'single happy path' for the prototype.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the one path still includes necessary platform scaffolding around the function: secret injection, default logs/metrics, and safe rollback hooks, because otherwise the path is not operationally real.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the one path only needs the customer-visible loop of uploading a function, wiring a trigger, and seeing it run successfully, with existing platform services treated as inherited background.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to simplify scope and use the same language of 'one path,' but each silently treats different parts of the system as so obviously inside or outside the slice that clarification never feels necessary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the prototype should show a credible 'pay-as-you-go' economics story.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this is satisfied if no tenant-specific compute is pre-provisioned and the serverless path is cheaper than current always-on workers for bursty traffic, even if some shared platform services retain steady baseline cost.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this is satisfied only if the customer-facing pilot narrative can honestly say idle tenants are effectively not paying for anything sitting around, without caveats about baseline shared services.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes straight from common serverless messaging, and both treat the omitted accounting details as background context rather than as something that must be surfaced in a brainstorm.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior 'spring sandbox' they plan to reuse
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to reuse 'the spring sandbox' to accelerate the prototype.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the March internal Firecracker-based isolation sandbox maintained by the platform infrastructure team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the April Knative-based demo sandbox that solutions engineering used for a partner-facing summit walkthrough.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both prototypes have been casually referred to in the organization as 'the sandbox from spring,' and each participant has a reason to think there is only one relevant prior experiment in view.

If this turns into a flashy story about serverless magic without the operational basics, we'll create expectations we can't meet. Best framing is event-driven customer code inside workflows, but with enough realism that it doesn't collapse in security review.
